intervals.label: excavation of the underground halls
intervals.locator: arXiv:1102.0208, paragraph 'Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), Italy'
intervals.note: L. Pandola (INFN LNGS) dates the start of the actual excavation to 1982 and its completion to 1987; the laboratory's own Italian description page also dates the start of the excavation of the underground halls to 1982 ('Le opere di scavo ... hanno avuto inizio nel 1982').
intervals.quote: After the initial proposal by the INFN President A. Zichichi in 1979, the actual excavation started in 1982, in coincidence with the freeway 10-km tunnel, and was completed in 1987.

intervals.label: laboratory operating
intervals.locator: arXiv:1102.0208, paragraph 'Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (LNGS), Italy'
intervals.note: The start of 1987 is the year the excavation of the underground halls was completed (L. Pandola, INFN LNGS, arXiv:1102.0208); no LNGS or INFN page consulted (checked 2026-10-28) states an opening date for the laboratory as such (lngs.infn.it/en/lab-history returned HTTP 404; the English overview gives no date), and a 2005 INFN presentation by E. Coccia says the first experiment, MACRO, started taking data in 1989, so the date the laboratory began operating is uncertain and 1987 is a lower bound. An undated interval would wrongly show the laboratory as not operating, although it clearly is ('Currently 1300 scientists from 30 different Countries are taking part in the experimental activities of LNGS', src:lngs-overview).
intervals.quote: After the initial proposal by the INFN President A. Zichichi in 1979, the actual excavation started in 1982, in coincidence with the freeway 10-km tunnel, and was completed in 1987.

name: Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso
notes: This record describes LNGS at a basic level (the laboratory and its Hall B, where ICARUS ran), not the full LNGS programme.

An m.w.e. overburden is not recorded as a spec here: the LNGS pages fetched give only the 1400 m rock thickness. L. Pandola's overview (arXiv:1102.0208) gives about 3100 m w.e. (minimum depth) and 3800 m w.e. (average depth), and the Borexino collaboration places Borexino at 3800 m w.e.

The foundation date of LNGS was not found on an official page; the excavation of the halls (1982-1987) is sourced to L. Pandola's overview (arXiv:1102.0208) and the laboratory's Italian description page, and the operating interval's start (1987) is the end of that excavation, marked uncertain.

operator.quote: LNGS is funded by the National Institute for Nuclear Physics (INFN), the Italian Institution in charge to coordinate and support research in elementary particles physics

depth.note: Stated as an average rock coverage; the mountain profile is asymmetric. No m.w.e. figure is given on the pages fetched.
depth.quote: The 1400 metre-rock thickness above the Laboratory represents a natural coverage that provides a cosmic ray flux reduction by one million times

summary.plain: The largest underground research laboratory in the world, built beside a motorway tunnel under the Gran Sasso mountain in central Italy. About 1400 metres of rock overhead cut the shower of cosmic particles by a factor of a million, which lets very quiet experiments run there.
summary.technical: INFN national laboratory at Assergi (L'Aquila), Italy, with three underground halls of roughly 100 × 20 × 18 m under about 1400 m of rock, hosting low-background neutrino, dark matter and double-beta-decay experiments; the ICARUS T600 ran in Hall B from 2010 to 2013.
